cards.question: What is the primary definition of an Object in OOP?
cards.answer: A software unit representing a real-world entity with state (attributes) and behavior (methods), encapsulating data and functionalities together.

cards.question: What is a Class in Object-Oriented Programming?
cards.answer: A blueprint, template, or prototype that defines the variables and methods common to all objects of that kind; objects are instances of a class.

cards.question: What is Encapsulation in OOP?
cards.answer: The OOP principle of bundling data and methods inside a single class and restricting direct access to internal state, exposing only public interfaces.

cards.question: What is Abstraction in OOP?
cards.answer: The process of exposing only essential features of an object while hiding complex background implementation details from the user.

cards.question: What is Inheritance in OOP?
cards.answer: A mechanism where a new class (subclass) derives characteristics and behaviors from an existing class (superclass), creating an IS-A relationship and enabling code reuse.

cards.question: What is Polymorphism in OOP?
cards.answer: The ability of an object or method call to take many forms, allowing different underlying forms to be processed through a single common interface.

cards.question: What is the Java Virtual Machine (JVM)?
cards.answer: An abstract computing machine that provides the runtime execution environment to convert platform-neutral Java bytecode into machine instructions.

cards.question: What is Java Bytecode?
cards.answer: The highly optimized intermediate set of instructions generated by the Java compiler (javac) and saved in .class files to be executed by the JVM.

cards.question: What does 'Write Once, Run Anywhere' (WORA) mean?
cards.answer: Java programs compile into architecture-neutral bytecode that can run without recompilation on any platform that has a compatible JVM installed.

cards.question: What are the four primary types of Java applications?
cards.answer: Standalone (desktop GUI/console) applications, Web applications, Enterprise applications (distributed/business), and Mobile applications.

cards.question: What does the 'new' keyword do in Java?
cards.answer: Dynamically allocates memory on the heap for a new object instance and calls the matching class constructor to initialize it.

cards.question: What is the difference between Instance and Static variables?
cards.answer: Instance variables belong to a specific object (each instance has a copy); static variables belong to the class itself and are shared across all instances.

cards.question: What is a Constructor in Java?
cards.answer: A special method with the same name as the class and no return type, invoked automatically to initialize a newly created object.

cards.question: What is Constructor Overloading?
cards.answer: Defining multiple constructors within the same class that have the same name but different parameter lists (count, type, or order).

cards.question: What is the 'this' keyword used for in Java?
cards.answer: It refers to the current object instance; used to resolve variable shadowing (this.x = x) or to call another constructor in the same class (this()).

cards.question: What are the four Access Modifiers in Java?
cards.answer: public (accessible everywhere), protected (same package + subclasses), default (package-private, same package only), and private (declaring class only).

cards.question: What is Method Overloading?
cards.answer: Defining multiple methods with the same name in the same class with different parameter lists; return type alone is not sufficient.

cards.question: How does Java manage memory with Garbage Collection?
cards.answer: The JVM automatically detects and reclaims heap memory occupied by objects that are no longer reachable by any active reference in the program.

cards.question: Why are Strings immutable in Java?
cards.answer: Once a String object is created, its sequence of characters cannot be modified; any modification creates a new String in memory for safety and caching.

cards.question: How do String literals differ from 'new String()'?
cards.answer: String literals are stored in the String Constant Pool to avoid duplicate instances; new String() always creates a new object in general heap memory.

cards.question: What is Inheritance and which keyword is used?
cards.answer: A mechanism where a subclass derives attributes and methods from a superclass using the extends keyword, facilitating code reuse.

cards.question: Why does Java disallow Multiple Inheritance with classes?
cards.answer: To avoid ambiguity such as the Diamond Problem where a subclass inherits conflicting implementations from two superclasses with identical method names.

cards.question: What is the java.lang.Object class?
cards.answer: The root class of the entire Java class hierarchy; every class in Java directly or indirectly extends Object and inherits its methods (e.g. equals, toString).

cards.question: How does the 'protected' modifier work across packages?
cards.answer: Protected members are accessible to all classes in the same package and to subclasses in different packages through inheritance.

cards.question: How are Superclass Constructors invoked in a Subclass?
cards.answer: Using super() or super(arguments), which must always be the very first statement inside the subclass constructor.

cards.question: What is Method Overriding in Java?
cards.answer: When a subclass provides a specific implementation for an instance method already defined in its superclass, using the same name, parameters, and return type.

cards.question: What is Method Hiding?
cards.answer: When a subclass defines a static method with the same signature as a superclass static method; it is resolved at compile time based on reference type.

cards.question: What is the purpose of the 'super' keyword?
cards.answer: It refers to the immediate superclass, allowing access to hidden superclass fields, overridden superclass methods (super.m()), and superclass constructors (super()).

cards.question: What does the 'final' keyword do when applied to a method?
cards.answer: It prevents the method from being overridden by any subclass, locking its implementation for security and optimization.

cards.question: What does the 'final' keyword do when applied to a class?
cards.answer: It prevents the class from being extended/subclassed by any other class (e.g., String is a final class).

cards.question: What are Compile-Time and Runtime Polymorphism?
cards.answer: Compile-time polymorphism is achieved via method overloading (static resolution); runtime polymorphism is achieved via method overriding (dynamic method dispatch).

cards.question: What is Dynamic Method Dispatch?
cards.answer: The mechanism where a call to an overridden method is resolved at runtime based on the actual object type in memory rather than the reference variable type.

cards.question: What is Upcasting in Java?
cards.answer: Assigning a subclass object reference to a superclass reference variable (e.g. Animal a = new Dog();), which is done automatically and safely.

cards.question: What is Downcasting and when is it used?
cards.answer: Casting a superclass reference back to its subclass type (e.g. Dog d = (Dog) a;), requiring an explicit cast; must be guarded by instanceof.

cards.question: What is an Abstract Class?
cards.answer: A class declared with abstract that cannot be instantiated with new; serves as a common template containing both abstract and concrete methods.

cards.question: What is an Abstract Method?
cards.answer: A method declared with abstract having only a signature and no body (abstract void m();), which must be implemented by concrete subclasses.

cards.question: What is an Interface in Java?
cards.answer: A reference type declared with interface defining abstract methods and constants (public static final) that classes implement using implements.

cards.question: How do Interfaces achieve Multiple Inheritance in Java?
cards.answer: A single class can implement multiple interfaces separated by commas (class C implements I1, I2), acquiring multiple behavioral contracts safely.

cards.question: What are Default Methods in interfaces?
cards.answer: Methods defined with the default keyword in interfaces that provide a default body, allowing interfaces to evolve without breaking existing implementing classes.

cards.question: Why do Interfaces promote Loose Coupling?
cards.answer: Components communicate through abstract contracts rather than concrete classes, allowing implementations to be replaced or modified without altering client code.

cards.question: What is an Exception in Java?
cards.answer: An abnormal condition or event that occurs during program execution and disrupts the normal instruction flow if left unhandled.

cards.question: What is the Throwable class hierarchy?
cards.answer: Throwable is the root of all errors and exceptions, branching into Error (serious JVM failures) and Exception (handleable conditions).

cards.question: How do Errors differ from Exceptions?
cards.answer: Errors (e.g. OutOfMemoryError) are fatal JVM conditions that cannot be recovered from programmatically; Exceptions are conditions applications can catch and handle.

cards.question: What are Checked Exceptions?
cards.answer: Exceptions checked at compile time (inherit from Exception but not RuntimeException); must be caught in try-catch or declared with throws.

cards.question: What are Unchecked Exceptions?
cards.answer: Subclasses of RuntimeException (e.g. NullPointerException, ArithmeticException) caused by programming logic bugs; not enforced at compile time.

cards.question: What is the role of the try and catch blocks?
cards.answer: try wraps code that might throw an exception; catch intercepts and handles specific exception types to prevent abnormal termination.

cards.question: What is the purpose of the finally block?
cards.answer: A block following try/catch that always executes (used for resource cleanup), regardless of whether an exception occurred or was handled.

cards.question: What is the difference between throw and throws?
cards.answer: throw explicitly triggers an exception object in code (throw new Exception()); throws declares in a method signature that the method may throw an exception.

cards.question: What is the ordering rule for Multiple Catch Blocks?
cards.answer: Specific subclass exception catch blocks must precede more general superclass catch blocks; otherwise the compiler flags unreachable code.

cards.question: How do you define a Custom User-Defined Exception?
cards.answer: By creating a class that extends Exception (for checked exceptions) or RuntimeException (for unchecked exceptions) and calling super(message).
